posts.content:
I’ve been splitting Google Search Console queries by word count lately to see how the mix of searches we appear for is changing.
 
Here are the custom regex filters I use:
 
1 word
^\S+$
 
2–4 words
^(\S+\s+){1,3}\S+$
 
5–10 words
^(\S+\s+){4,9}\S+$
 
11–20 words
^(\S+\s+){10,19}\S+$
 
21+ words
^(\S+\s+){20,}\S+$
 
And for queries that start like questions:
 
^(who|what|when|where|why|how|which|can|does|do|is|are|should|will)\b
 
You can paste these into GSC under Query → Custom (regex), then export each group and analyze them with AI.
 
Why?
 
Because a 2-word query and a 20-word query usually represent very different searches.
 
Shorter queries tend to be categories, products, brands, or broad topics.
 
As queries get longer, you start seeing much more context like use cases, constraints, comparisons, problems, and full questions that sound surprisingly similar to what buyers ask on sales calls.
 
That makes the YoY comparison interesting too.
 
In the image, my client is now getting nearly 25× more impressions from 11–20-word queries than at the same point last year. (yes, I know, ZERO clicks  👁️)
 
And no, these don’t seem to be weird AI-looking strings. They’re searches like:
 
“which [insert SaaS category] products in the united states come with licenses and regulatory compliance?”
 
That gives me a quick way to isolate the most specific searches and look for content opportunities inside them.
 
If Google is already showing one of my pages for a 17-word question I only answer indirectly, that’s a pretty good clue that I should probably answer it properly.
 
And if the same question keeps showing up in sales calls? Even better.

posts.content:
It took me ~15 minutes to build this month's GEO plan for a client. P.S.: What could I have done differently here? any tips?  👁️ 

  🤖  1.     I pulled 30 recorded sales calls

  🤖  2.     I gave the transcripts to Claude and asked it to pull out the questions prospects asked, in the words they used

It filtered out demo questions, scheduling questions, and other noise, and left me with roughly 50 real buyer questions.

  🤖  3.     Then I tested every question across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, and Google AI Mode. I used temporary or incognito sessions where possible to reduce personalization from my own search history.

For each one, I wanted to know:

Are we being cited?
Are we being recommended?
Or are we completely missing from the answer?

Ahrefs Brand Radar can automate a lot of this, and I love it, but it’s expensive. If you have the budget, use it, I find it better than Semrush's AI tracking features.

The manual check still gave me something useful very quickly.

Turns out my client is showing up well for TOFU searches where people already understood the category. But we're much weaker on pain-related questions, those questions people ask when they know they have a problem, but they don’t know what kind of solution they need yet.

So if someone already knows the category, we have a good chance of showing up.
If they’re still trying to understand what’s causing their problem or what they should even do about it, we’re much harder to find.

That gave me a very obvious content gap.

  🤖  4.     I asked Claude to build a plan around the gaps.

It prioritized questions where:

> we weren’t showing up
> the buyer intent was strong
> and the topic was relevant to what my client sells

Those went to the top of the list.

  🤖  5.     Within 5 minutes, I was already updating existing content and had a month-long GEO optimization plan that could run alongside the content calendar I already had.

The biggest takeaway for me was where the strategy started.

It started with real questions from real prospects. If Sales hadn’t given me access to those call recordings, I probably would’ve built the plan around keyword data, competitor content, or questions that AI thought buyers might ask.

Those can all be useful inputs, but the sales calls showed me the exact language prospects were already using while evaluating the problem.

That made the rest of the GEO work much easier to prioritize.

posts.content:
One thing I find interesting about ABM is how much of the work happens where almost nobody sees it. The account research, ICP decisions, data cleanup, enrichment, segmentation, scoring, orchestration, and constant testing usually sit far behind the campaign itself. If everything works, the outside world only sees a relevant message reaching the right person at the right time. That is probably a good sign for the campaign, but it also means a lot of the knowledge marketers develop stays hidden with the work.

I think that creates an interesting contradiction for marketers. We spend our days helping companies build positioning, communicate expertise, create authority, and become more recognizable in their markets. Then, when it comes to doing the same for ourselves, many of us barely know where to start. Personal branding can feel like self-promotion, especially when your instinct is to focus on the work rather than talk about it. So we keep learning, solving problems, and building experience without necessarily making any of that visible.

But your personal brand does not have to be about having the loudest opinions on LinkedIn. It can simply be a record of how you think. The frameworks you use. The mistakes you have made. The campaigns that changed your perspective. The small lessons you picked up after cleaning 5,000 rows of account data or realizing that the targeting strategy mattered more than the copy. Sharing those things consistently gives people context for what you know, what you care about, and what kind of marketer you are becoming.

So this is something I am trying to practice more intentionally: document what I learn instead of waiting until I have something “important” to say. Pick a few areas you genuinely want to be associated with. Turn the problems you solve at work into lessons others can use. Share an opinion when experience has actually given you one. And, most importantly, do it consistently. You do not need to manufacture a personal brand. You need to make enough of your thinking visible for your own voice to eventually emerge.

posts.content:
Yesterday I gave my AI revenue sculpting system one instruction.

Read the last 120 days of my email, Slack, and CRM before answering any prompt, so every answer I get is answered in context, making my output 10X better.

It sounded obviously right when I said it, and more context does usually mean better answers.

Then I looked at how much data the instruction would actually have to read every time, and the literal version was impossible to build.

My CRM holds 36,436 deal records as of this morning. Slack hands the system back twenty search results at a time. The email window alone held 201 threads when it got measured yesterday.

Evaluating all of that before answering one question I was prompting it for would take minutes per prompt, and the answer would come back as AI slop, buried under context that has nothing to do with the question.

That was honestly a little humbling, because the instruction was mine, and the data against it came out of the connectors I told the system to check every time I prompt.

So now the system runs it in two layers instead.

A small ledger, about 14 kilobytes, rebuilt on a routine every morning at 6:12 am, carries every open deal, every counterparty, and every open loop I haven't checked yet, and it is only trusted to say where to look.

Before the system states anything as a fact, it opens the live record: the deal, the thread, the calendar invite.

The reason for the split is that a summary written yesterday is a memory, and between yesterday's count and this morning's, the same CRM added twelve deal records.

If you're a founder wiring AI into your revenue motion, you've probably given it some version of my instruction: "know everything about my company, and always answer me with the full context of my situation."

Stored context earns its place by pointing at the right record, and the live data is what will provide the best answer.

Ask your AI where the number in its last answer came from. If it probably will give a stored summary it never checked against the live record, you now know which of its answers need a second look.

posts.content:
A rebrand doesn’t always mean starting over!

I was on a client call going over a rebrand process and we got into a conversation I’ve been thinking about since.

When you start a rebrand, there’s a natural temptation to look at the existing identity and immediately think about what you’d do differently. But before changing anything, I think there’s value in asking a different question:

Why was it done this way in the first place?

The brand we were looking at had a lot behind it. There were decisions around the audience, the business, the positioning, the visual language. Someone had already done the work. Someone had already made the calls, but that doesn’t mean everything has to stay.

Brands change. Companies grow. Sometimes what worked a few years ago doesn’t quite fit anymore. A product expands, the audience shifts, the business starts to see itself differently.

And that’s where the idea of evolution comes in.

A rebrand doesn’t have to erase what came before. Sometimes it’s about looking closely at what already exists and figuring out what still feels true.

Maybe the color stays, but the way you use it changes. Maybe the logo stays recognizable, but the system around it becomes more flexible. Maybe part of the visual language no longer makes sense at all.

I’ve started to think that the interesting part of a rebrand lives somewhere in between preserving and changing, instead of trying to move the brand forward without pretending the previous chapter never happened, and honestly, that feels like a much natural way to approach the work.

Stop writing newsletters nobody opens.

The problem usually isn't your writing. It's that you're writing about your product instead of your reader's problem.

A newsletter has to earn the word news. That means current tools, new strategies, and information your reader hasn't seen five other places already.

Pick one specific problem or workflow per issue. Not a broad theme, a specific thing your reader is stuck on this week.

Then pack it with enough detail that they can act on it today. If someone can't finish your newsletter and immediately go do something, you buried the value too deep.

Aim for one implementable idea per send, not ten shallow ones.

What's the last newsletter that made you actually go do something?
